what: Brunswick is the world’s largest maker of recreational boats and marine engines. It owns Mercury Marine outboard engines and boat brands such as Sea Ray, Boston Whaler, Bayliner and Lund, and sells parts, accessories and boat club memberships.
customers: Recreational boaters, mostly in North America, buying through independent dealers; also boat builders that use Mercury engines.
money: Outboard and sterndrive engines sold with Brunswick boats and to other boat builders.
Fibreglass and aluminium boats across many price levels.
Replacement parts, electronics and boat club memberships, which are steadier than new boat sales.
moat: Mercury is the leading outboard engine brand, and its share of the large-horsepower engines that buyers now favour gives Brunswick a strong position. The dealer network and parts business add recurring revenue.
risks: Boats are expensive discretionary purchases, and higher interest rates have hit demand hard: revenue fell from $6.8B in 2022 to $5.2B in 2024.
Dealers cut their inventories, so Brunswick’s shipments fell faster than retail sales.
2025 showed a net loss of $137M, largely from charges, while operating cash flow was still $562M.
Debt of $2.2B against $1.7B of equity is significant for a cyclical company.
opportunities: Trailing revenue of $5.7B is rising again, which suggests the inventory correction is ending.
Free cash flow stayed positive throughout the downturn, $264M in 2024 and $396M in 2025.
Lower interest rates would make boat loans cheaper and lift demand.
Sixteen analysts average a target of $88, about 22% above the price.
watch: Retail boat sales and dealer inventory levels, which together show when shipments can grow again.
view: Brunswick is a cyclical company coming out of a hard downturn. Revenue fell by almost a quarter from 2022 to 2024 as rate rises made boat loans expensive and dealers cut their stock, and 2025 ended with a loss after charges. The reported numbers look poor, but the cash did not: free cash flow stayed positive every year and was nearly $400 million in 2025.

That is the key to valuing it. At $4.6 billion, the market pays around 12 times that cash flow for the leading engine maker and boat builder in a market that is just turning. The trailing revenue of $5.7 billion, well above 2025’s $5.4 billion, suggests shipments are recovering.

The investment turns on interest rates and consumer confidence, because a boat is one of the first purchases people delay. If rates keep falling, Brunswick can earn far more than today on a recovering market, and the shares are reasonably priced for that. If the consumer weakens, they can fall a lot further. I think the cycle is turning, but I would size this as a cyclical position, not a core holding.
bull: Lower rates revive boat demand, dealers restock and Mercury’s strong share lifts earnings well above today’s level.
bear: Consumers stay cautious, the recovery stalls and debt limits Brunswick’s room to manoeuvre.
